newsitem.title: FRANCE: French parties, media split over far-right Le Pen.
newsitem.headline: French parties, media split over far-right Le Pen.

text.p: Ban him? Prosecute him? Legislate against him? Debate him? Demonstrate against him? Report on him? Ignore him? Fight him in the streets?
France's political establishment and media are deeply divided over how to counter the seemingly inexorable rise of extreme-right anti-immigration crusader Jean-Marie Le Pen.

As Le Pen basks in the glare of publicity ahead of his National Front (FN) party's congress in Strasbourg this weekend, the mainstream parties, newspapers and broadcasters are anxiously debating how to deal with him.
France's left-wing parties, reinforced by young Socialists from across western Europe, plan to demonstrate against Le Pen in Strasbourg on Saturday.
Intellectual anti-fascist groups have chartered "freedom trains" to take celebrities and activists to Strasbourg from Paris and Toulon, the biggest city run by the National Front.
Le Pen says he is convinced left-wing agitation against him plays into the FN's hands by outraging ordinary voters.
The debate often degenerates into a left-right blame-game. Conservatives accuse the Socialists of having opened the doors of television studios and parliament to Le Pen in the 1980s.
The left accuses the centre-right of adopting the Front's political agenda by passing repressive immigration laws.
After Le Pen openly espoused racial inequality last year, opposition Socialist politician Henri Emmanuelli called for the FN to be banned.

But his own party disowned the idea and few politicians believe it is feasible now that Le Pen has 15 percent of the vote and holds seats in the European Parliament, regional assemblies and city councils across France.

Conservative Gaullist Justice Minister Jacques Toubon has proposed a tougher bill to punish racist statements, but his own coalition shows no sign of willingness to enact legislation which critics say would make a martyr of Le Pen.

Pierre Mazeaud, Gaullist chairman of parliament's legal committee, says the government could and should prosecute Le Pen under existing laws on incitement to racial hatred. Toubon says experts have advised him prospects of a conviction are slight.
The parliamentary leader of the centre-right UDF party, Gilles de Robien, called this week for a "media boycott" of the National Front, an idea immediately rejected by the media.

"I am exasperated by the direct or indirect publicity given to an extremist group for months. The political class should get a grip on itself and the media should erect a wall of silence against a group which is antidemocratic," he said.
With few exceptions, media editors reject such ideas, arguing that the public must be informed about the Front's ideas if they are to recognise a danger.
Many argue that most Germans were unaware of Adolf Hitler's anti-semitic creed until after he came to power in 1933.
They are determined no one should be able to say they did not know Le Pen advocated expelling three million immigrants.
Anne Sinclair, France's most popular television interviewer, has consistently refused to have Le Pen on her weekly programme.

Another popular television interviewer, Christine Ockrent, tried to confront Le Pen when he appeared on her show last year, interrupting and provoking him, but the politician was widely seen to have emerged the winner.
At a public meeting in Strasbourg on Wednesday, Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy said the more other politicians attacked the Front, the more its gained popularity.
"I warn against any violence which the Front congress could spark. That would only benefit the Front which awaits rather than fears it," Douste-Blazy said.
